fixes.explanation: No warning in sight, friend. Laban says, “I have learned by divination that the LORD has blessed me because of you.” That's a man who checked his books and found Jacob's name all over the good numbers. Nobody walks up to someone like that and says “Name your wages” if the news was bad.

A test isn't what Laban says. He asks Jacob to stay first: “If I have found favor in your eyes, please stay.” Then he gives his reason: “I have learned by divination that the LORD has blessed me because of you.” I think Laban just did the math and didn't like the answer he got when he pictured Jacob leaving.

Kindness is a lovely word, but Jacob reaches for a different one. He says, “…my honesty will testify for me…” and then draws the line: any goats that are not speckled or spotted, or lambs that are not dark-colored, “…will be considered stolen.” That's a man handing his boss a ruler and saying, “Measure me.” I've had friends who wouldn't do that with a single cookie crumb.

Laban takes out the streaked or spotted male goats, the speckled or spotted female goats and every dark-colored lamb, and places them “…under the care of his sons.” Those are Laban's own sons. Notice it all happens “That very day…” and he doesn't wait around. I think a man that quick knows exactly what he's doing.

Jacob's sons are a good guess, but the text says Laban put the animals “…under the care of his sons.” That's Laban's own household. Picture it like handing your last tray of cookies to your cousin so the person who asked for them can't reach the plate. Laban keeps those animals in the family, and then he puts three days of road between them and Jacob (Genesis 30:36).

Green sap makes sense if you're picturing a fresh branch, and these are fresh ones. But the text says Jacob peeled the bark, “…exposing the white inner wood of the branches.” White, friend, like a pale stripe on a dark stick. He lined those up at the watering troughs where the flocks would see them.

Dark wood is a fair guess, but the color is the other way around. The text says Jacob peeled the bark, “…exposing the white inner wood of the branches.” So the branches had pale stripes where the bark came off. Then he set them in the watering troughs in front of the flocks.

That's right, it's False, and Jacob is careful about it. The text says he “…set his own stock apart and did not put them with Laban’s animals.” Two flocks, two sets of animals, and he keeps a clear line between them. Honestly, I've never kept my sprinkles and my chocolate chips that organized.

Thirsty is a good guess, since these branches sit in the watering troughs. But the verse says, “…if the animals were weak, he did not set out the branches.” Strength is what Jacob checks, not thirst. The text says the weaker animals went to Laban and the stronger ones to Jacob (Genesis 30:42).
